definition.text: The Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora, a treaty that protects endangered plants and animals from the threats of international trade.

facts.text: Its text was agreed by 80 countries in Washington, D.C. on 3 March 1973, and it entered into force on 1 July 1975.
It is legally binding on its Parties, but each must pass its own laws to apply it nationally.
It works by controlling trade in listed species as they cross borders, including products made from them such as traditional medicines.
Over 40,900 species, subspecies and populations are protected.
It works as a negative list: trade in any species is unregulated unless it is listed, so many species are traded with no review.
Critics say it ignores habitat loss and poverty and does not address market demand; listings can even increase speculation in high-value species.
As of 2002, 50% of Parties lacked one or more of its four major implementation requirements.

definition.text: The three CITES lists that rank protected species by how much international trade threatens them, and set the trade controls that apply.

facts.text: Appendix I species face extinction: commercial trade in wild specimens is banned and other trade needs both import and export permits.
Appendix II species are not necessarily threatened but need controlled trade; most listed taxa are here and need an export permit.
Appendix III species are protected in at least one country that has asked other Parties to help control trade.
Captive-bred specimens of Appendix I species may be traded as if they were Appendix II.

definition.text: Harmful encounters between people and wild animals, with bad results both for people and their property and for wildlife and its habitat.

facts.text: It comes from competition between people and wildlife for natural resources, and has grown with population growth and changing land use.
Consequences include destroyed crops, livestock killed by predators, human injury and death, damaged infrastructure and disease spread.
Crop damage by elephants can lead locals to kill elephants in retaliation; in Sri Lanka up to 80 people and over 230 elephants die each year.
Hidden costs include health impacts, opportunity costs and transaction costs.
Fear of predators can worsen conflict more than the actual damage done.

definition.text: The methods used to reduce harmful encounters between people and wildlife, from fences and guard dogs to paying people for their losses.

facts.text: The most successful solutions involve local communities in planning, implementation and maintenance.
Some governments pay compensation for wildlife losses to discourage retaliatory killing; results vary because of under-payment and late payment.
Livestock-guarding dogs cut animal losses to on average 60 times lower than the norm.
Moving problem animals elsewhere is largely ineffective and can harm the species.

title: Ivory trade

definition.text: The commercial, often illegal trade in the tusks of elephants and of other animals such as hippopotamus, walrus and narwhal.

facts.text: Elephant ivory has been exported from Africa and Asia for millennia; at its colonial-era peak 800 to 1,000 tonnes a year went to Europe alone.
African elephants fell from about 1.3 million in 1979 to 600,000 in 1989, with around 75,000 killed each year for ivory worth about 1 billion dollars.
The main threat turned out to be the international ivory trade rather than habitat loss.
Southern African states opposed the 1990 ban, saying their elephant herds were well managed and ivory revenue funded conservation.
Zimbabwe and others argued wildlife needs economic value to survive and local communities must be involved.
In 1997 CITES let Botswana, Namibia and Zimbabwe sell 49 tonnes of registered stockpiles to Japan as an "experiment".
The piano industry abandoned ivory keys in the 1980s for plastic, and synthetic ivory now exists.

contested_note: States disagree on whether a total ban or regulated sales that fund conservation best protect elephants.

definition.text: A family of software for systematic reserve design that finds networks of sites meeting biodiversity targets at low cost.

facts.text: It uses simulated annealing to minimise the total cost of a reserve system while representing a set share of each feature.
Computationally it solves a conservation version of the 0-1 knapsack problem.
It is the most widely used conservation planning software, used for systems covering about 5% of Earth's surface, including the Great Barrier Reef reserve network.
Exact integer programming tools such as prioritizr guarantee optimal solutions and can find cheaper ones faster.

definition.text: A protected area that exists on paper but has little real management or protection on the ground.

facts.text: It can result from weak governance, weak regulations or lack of enforcement.
A 2020 study of 3,449 European marine protected areas found 70% faced at least one significant threat and 86% of the network was hit by damaging fishing gear.

definition.text: Planning a nature reserve's size, shape, location and links so that it actually achieves its goal of protecting biodiversity.

facts.text: Planners must weigh habitat preferences, migration, climate change and public support.
A reserve set up where people depend on the land for their livelihood often fails, as when Bolivia's expanded Amboró park later had to be shrunk.
Too-small reserves bring carnivores into contact with people, raising their mortality.
Reserve networks linked by wildlife corridors protect species that migrate, and can raise movement between patches by up to 50%.
To be cost-effective, reserves should be placed in species-rich places such as biodiversity hotspots.
Designs must allow for future ranges, since 80% of observed range shifts have moved polewards or upward at an average of 6.1 km per decade.

title: Integrated Conservation and Development Project

definition.text: A biodiversity conservation project that also invests in rural development, so that local people gain from protecting nature.

facts.text: WWF introduced them in the mid-1980s to fix problems with the non-participatory "fines and fences" approach.
They are usually tied to a protected area and funded from outside by conservation and development agencies.
They assume that more varied livelihoods will ease human pressure on biodiversity.
Critics say projects were designed with little local input and rarely share costs and benefits with women and minority groups.
They can overlook outside pressures such as market demand and illegal logging, and may collapse when external funding ends.

contested_note: WWF says its projects work with local organisations, while critics say they exclude local voices and can harm communities.

title: Conservation triage

definition.text: The idea that not every species can be saved, so conservationists must choose which ones to spend their limited efforts on.

facts.text: The pressure comes from extinction threats estimated at 15 to 37 percent of all species by 2050.
Critics say "endangered species triage" decides which species to let go instead of re-examining the economics driving the decline.

contested_note: Supporters see triage as realistic priority-setting, while rights-of-nature critics say it accepts losses instead of changing the economics behind them.
